content: If a case is incorrectly de-notified, it is re-notified. If the treatment provided was inadequate, the national team recommends a follow-up appointment that includes clinical assessment and appropriate diagnostic testing. Laboratories are followed up for missing or future specimen dates and drug susceptibility testing (DST) results. Cross-referencing is conducted with prison health logs to identify prisoners who were not notified or to correct unreported risk factors. Mortality data is cross-referenced with the mortality registry to ensure accuracy. Clinics are followed up for missing data or notifications for patients in molecular clusters as part of the national strain typing service. The UK system met two out of three benchmarks. However, it was not possible to determine whether the completeness benchmark for bacteriological confirmation was met, and thus the standard is considered partially met. In the United States, there are 60 reporting areas, both within and outside the country, that either use their own software or opt for CDC-generated software to report tuberculosis (TB) case data to the CDC. Those using CDC applications have built-in electronic validation rules defined by the CDC. Areas using their own software may or may not apply validation rules, but they are encouraged to adopt CDC-standardized validation rules. The CDC receives limited patient identifiers, such as date of birth, sex, and a unique state case number issued by the reporting areas. Full identifying information is maintained at the state and local levels, where legal custody and authority over such information reside. The CDC has developed data quality assurance resources, including guidelines, flowcharts, tools, training courses, and self-study modules for staff in reporting areas. The 60 reporting areas submit annual data files to a central database managed by the CDC. Upon receipt, 211 validation rules are applied to the data. These rules include requirements such as the state case number being alphanumeric and unique, dates of birth being after January 1, 1890, and other specific criteria for test results, dates, and anatomical codes. If data fail to meet any of these rules, an error report is sent back to the reporting jurisdiction for correction and resubmission. Once revised data are received, additional rules are applied to produce a clean dataset for analysis and reporting. Uncorrected data are replaced with blanks during the cleaning process. The CDC provides feedback to reporting jurisdictions through two limited-access websites. One reports completeness indicators for selected data items based on the National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) objectives and performance targets. The other, accessible to state-level TB program managers and CDC TB surveillance personnel, shows line-listed data of missing variables for individual TB cases. The CDC requests that all variables in the standard reporting form (Report of Verified Case of TB) be 95% complete when reported at year-end. Variables such as age, sex, year of registration, bacteriological results, history of previous treatment, and anatomical site of disease were all ≥95% complete. De-duplication is the responsibility of each jurisdiction, and no checks for duplicates are conducted on the national dataset, as it does not include patient names or addresses. Each case is assigned a unique number by the state, and the software warns users if a previously assigned number is reused. Jurisdictions also have written protocols to alert each other when a patient moves between jurisdictions to prevent duplicate reporting at the national level. The USA system met two out of three benchmarks. However, it was not possible to determine whether the benchmark on de-duplication at the national level was met, and thus the standard is considered partially met. The evaluation of external consistency of data should be an integral part of assessing any TB surveillance system. National and sub-national TB surveillance data are compared against plausible ranges of values based on global TB epidemiology. For example, a relatively small proportion of TB cases occur among children, and the percentage of cases among children can indicate the level of recent infection in a country or the performance of the surveillance system in capturing diagnosed childhood TB cases. To assess benchmarks, national surveillance data from the most recent year with complete data should be analyzed to determine the percentage of new TB cases aged <15 years among all new TB cases. The ranges of values used for benchmarks are based on recent observations from national surveillance data and TB epidemiological studies. However, some countries with accurate data and high-performing surveillance systems may fall outside these ranges. Having values within the stated benchmark ranges provides reassurance of a well-functioning surveillance system, satisfying the benchmark and meeting the standard. In settings with accurate data and high-performing systems, alternative explanations for deviations should be considered and documented. For countries without vital registration (VR) data, benchmarks for internal consistency are included based on data that most countries should collect. These benchmarks include ratios of pulmonary to extrapulmonary TB cases, male-to-female TB case ratios, proportions of childhood TB cases, year-to-year changes in case notification rates, and other indicators. Trends in case counts are expected to align with trends in measured TB mortality. For countries with VR data, a five-year trend can be analyzed using linear regression of log-transformed rates over time. The slope represents the average rate of change per year, and the sign of the slope indicates the trend direction. The benchmark is met if the slope for case notification rates aligns with the slope for TB mortality rates. In countries without VR data, national-level TB case data disaggregated by age, sex, and type of disease, along with notification rates, are required for the past five years. Sub-national data should also be collected and examined. Childhood TB cases (0–14 years) should be reported for all forms of TB. If data for all forms of childhood TB are unavailable, the proportion of new smear-positive cases in children can be used. Some countries may have registries listing individuals with presumptive TB, providing an indication of the total number referred for diagnostic testing. For VR-recorded deaths with ill-defined causes, it can be assumed that the proportion of deaths attributable to TB is the same as the observed proportion in recorded deaths with well-defined causes. Adjusted TB mortality rates from VR systems can be obtained online from WHO. If this benchmark can be assessed, there is no need to assess the other six benchmarks, although such analyses can provide additional insights.
